chapters.name: Chapter 1: Clean hands and clean food

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Handwashing and personal hygiene
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Wash your hands the right way at the right times and follow basic hygiene rules.
This lesson builds toward: During a kitchen shift, you will wash your hands the right way at the right times and keep bare hands off ready-to-eat food, scrubbing for at least 20 seconds and naming at least six times to wash. Before and during a job in food service, you will identify the illness symptoms you must report and find the food handler card rule where you work, naming the symptoms and the deadline, card length and accepted courses from your health department.
Hands spread more foodborne illness than almost anything else. Wash them in a handwashing sink (never a food prep or dish sink) with warm running water and soap. Scrub hands, between fingers, under nails and up the wrists for at least 20 seconds, rinse, and dry with a single-use paper towel or a hand dryer. Use the towel to turn off the tap if the sink has handles.
Wash when you start work, after using the restroom, after touching raw meat, poultry or seafood, after touching your face, hair, phone or trash, after eating, drinking, smoking or coughing, after cleaning, and before putting on gloves. Gloves do not replace handwashing, and you change them when they tear, when you switch tasks, and after handling raw food.
Do not touch ready-to-eat food (food that will not be cooked again, like salad, bread or a cooked burger) with bare hands. Use gloves, tongs, deli paper or utensils.
Personal hygiene: wear clean clothes and a hair restraint, keep nails short and clean, and cover cuts with a bandage and a glove. Tell your manager if you have vomiting, diarrhea, yellow skin or eyes (jaundice), or a sore throat with fever, or if you are diagnosed with certain illnesses such as norovirus, hepatitis A or salmonella. You may need to stay home or away from food.
Step by step:
- Use the handwashing sink only.
- Wet hands with warm running water and add soap.
- Scrub hands, fingers, nails and wrists for at least 20 seconds.
- Rinse, and dry with a paper towel or hand dryer.
- Turn off the tap with the towel.
- Put on new gloves if handling ready-to-eat food.
Words to know:
- Foodborne illness: sickness caused by eating food that has germs or toxins in it.
- Ready-to-eat food: food that will be eaten without more cooking, such as salad, bread or a cooked burger.
- Jaundice: yellowing of the skin or eyes, a sign of illnesses such as hepatitis A.
Official sources:
- FDA: Safe food handling (handwashing for at least 20 seconds)
- FDA: Food Code 2022
Try it now: Wash your hands the full way while timing yourself: at least 20 seconds of scrubbing. Then write down six times during a kitchen shift when you must wash your hands.
You can now wash your hands correctly, know when to wash, avoid bare-hand contact with ready-to-eat food, and know which symptoms to report.

options: Food that will not be cooked again, like salad or bread
Raw chicken waiting to be cooked
Frozen food in the freezer
Any food in a sealed package
check.why: Ready-to-eat food will not be cooked again, so it must not touch bare hands.

check.q: You just took out the trash and now need to make a sandwich. What do you do first?
options: Put on gloves right away
Wash your hands, then put on new gloves
Wipe your hands on your apron
Use hand sanitizer only
check.why: Gloves do not replace handwashing; you wash after touching trash and before putting on gloves.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Preventing cross-contamination
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Store and prepare food so germs and allergens do not spread from one food or surface to another.
This lesson builds toward: Given raw and ready-to-eat foods to store or prepare, you will store and prepare them so germs do not spread, putting every item on the right cooler shelf and using separate or sanitized tools.
Cross-contamination is when germs move from one thing to another: from raw chicken to a salad, from a dirty cutting board to bread, or from your hands to a sandwich.
Keep raw and ready-to-eat food apart. Use separate cutting boards, knives and utensils for raw meat and for produce or cooked food; many kitchens use color-coded boards. If you must use the same surface, clean and sanitize it between tasks.
Store food the right way in the cooler. Keep ready-to-eat food on the top shelves. Store raw animal foods below, in order of their cooking temperature: whole cuts and fish above ground meat, and poultry on the bottom, so juices cannot drip onto foods that need less cooking. Cover and label food with the name and date.
Other habits: never put cooked food back on a plate or tray that held raw meat; keep chemicals away from and below food; and use a clean scoop, not a glass or your hand, for ice.
Step by step:
- Use separate boards and knives for raw meat and ready-to-eat food.
- Clean and sanitize surfaces between tasks.
- Store ready-to-eat food on top in the cooler.
- Store raw meat below: whole cuts and fish, then ground meat, then poultry at the bottom.
- Cover and label stored food with name and date.
- Keep chemicals away from and below food.
Words to know:
- Cross-contamination: when germs or allergens move from one food, surface or hand to another food.
- Color-coded boards: cutting boards in different colors for different foods, to keep them apart.
Official sources:
- FDA: Safe food handling (separate raw and ready-to-eat food)
Try it now: Draw a cooler with four shelves. Place these items on the right shelves: a tray of raw chicken thighs, a container of cut lettuce, raw ground beef, and raw salmon fillets. Write one sentence saying why the order matters.
You can now store and prepare food so germs do not spread between raw and ready-to-eat items.

options: Cooking food too long
Storing food in a freezer
Germs moving from one food or surface to another
Mixing two sauces together
check.why: Cross-contamination is when germs move from one thing, like raw chicken, to another.

check.q: You need ice for drinks. What do you use to scoop it?
options: A drinking glass
Your clean hand
A cup from the dish rack
A clean ice scoop
check.why: A clean scoop keeps hands and broken glass out of the ice.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Allergens and cleaning versus sanitizing
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Serve a guest with a food allergy safely and clean and sanitize a surface correctly.
This lesson builds toward: When a guest has a food allergy or a surface needs cleaning, you will follow the allergy steps and clean and sanitize a surface in the right order, with every step in order and no guessing about ingredients.
A food allergy can kill. The FDA names nine major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish (such as shrimp and crab), tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added on January 1, 2023.
When a guest says they have an allergy, take it seriously. Tell the manager or the chef. Check the recipe and the labels of every ingredient. Wash your hands, change gloves, and use clean and sanitized equipment and surfaces to make the food. Keep it apart from other food and deliver it separately. If you are not sure the dish is safe, say so; never guess. If a guest has signs of a reaction, such as trouble breathing or swelling, call 911.
Cleaning and sanitizing are different. Cleaning removes food, dirt and grease that you can see. Sanitizing reduces germs to safe levels. You must clean first; sanitizer does not work well on a dirty surface.
To clean and sanitize a prep table: scrape off food, wash with soap and water, rinse, apply sanitizer at the right strength (check with the test strips your kitchen uses and the label directions), leave it on for the contact time on the label, and let it air dry. Do not wipe it dry with a towel. Dishes in a three-compartment sink follow the same order: wash, rinse, sanitize, air dry.
Step by step:
- Allergy: tell the manager or chef and check every ingredient.
- Wash hands, change gloves, use clean and sanitized tools.
- Keep the allergy order apart and deliver it separately.
- Surface: scrape, wash, rinse.
- Sanitize at the right strength (test strips) for the label's contact time.
- Air dry; do not towel dry.
Words to know:
- Allergen: a food that can cause a dangerous immune reaction in some people.
- Sanitizing: reducing germs on a clean surface to safe levels with heat or a chemical.
- Contact time: how long a sanitizer must stay wet on a surface to work.
- Test strips: paper strips that show whether a sanitizer solution is the right strength.
Official sources:
- FDA: Food allergies (the nine major food allergens)
Try it now: Pick a menu item you know, such as a cheeseburger or a stir-fry. List which of the nine major allergens it might contain. Then write the six steps you would follow to clean and sanitize the prep table after making it.
You can now handle an allergy order safely and clean and sanitize a surface in the right order.

check.q: Why must you clean a surface before you sanitize it?
options: Sanitizer does not work well on a dirty surface
Cleaning makes the sanitizer smell better
Sanitizing removes grease by itself
Cleaning is only needed once a week
check.why: Sanitizer needs a clean surface to reduce germs to safe levels.

check.q: A guest asks if a dish has sesame and you are not sure. What do you say?
options: "It should be fine."
"I am not sure; let me check with the chef and the labels."
"Just pick the sesame out."
"Nobody is allergic to sesame."
check.why: Never guess about allergens; check the recipe and labels with the chef or manager.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The temperature danger zone
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep cold food cold and hot food hot, and check temperatures with a thermometer.
This lesson builds toward: Given cold and hot TCS food and a thermometer, you will check holding temperatures and thaw food safely, cold at 41°F or below and hot at 135°F or above, every time.
Germs grow fastest between 41°F and 135°F. This range is called the temperature danger zone. In food service, the FDA Food Code says to hold cold food at 41°F or below and hot food at 135°F or above. (Home cooking advice from the FDA and USDA uses 40°F and 140°F; at work, follow the code your health department uses.)
Foods that need this control are called TCS foods (time/temperature control for safety): meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked rice, beans and potatoes, cut melons, cut tomatoes, cut leafy greens, tofu and sprouts, among others.
Use a clean, sanitized food thermometer. Put the tip in the thickest part of the food, not touching bone or the pan. Check holding temperatures on a schedule, such as every 2 hours, and write them on the log. Calibrate the thermometer as your kitchen trains you.
Thaw food safely: in the cooler, under cold running water, in the microwave if it will be cooked right away, or as part of cooking. Never thaw food on the counter.
Step by step:
- Clean and sanitize the thermometer.
- Put the tip in the thickest part of the food.
- Cold food: 41°F or below. Hot food: 135°F or above.
- Write the reading and time on the log.
- If food is in the danger zone, tell your manager.
Words to know:
- Temperature danger zone: 41°F to 135°F in food service: the range where germs grow fastest.
- TCS food: food that needs time and temperature control to stay safe, such as meat, dairy, cooked rice and cut melon.
- Calibrate: check and adjust a thermometer so it reads correctly.
Official sources:
- FDA: Key temperatures for egg safety in food service (41°F cold holding, 135°F hot holding)
- FDA: Food Code 2022
Try it now: Use a food thermometer at home or work to check the temperature inside your refrigerator (put it in a glass of water in the fridge for a few minutes) and of one hot food. Write down whether each is safe for food service holding.
You can now name the temperature danger zone, keep TCS food out of it, and check temperatures correctly.

options: Food that is always served cold
Food that comes in a can
Food that needs time and temperature control for safety
Food that is only sold in stores
check.why: TCS food needs time and temperature control because germs can grow in it.

check.q: A hot-holding pan of beans reads 120°F at the 2-hour check. What do you do?
options: Write it down and keep serving
Add more beans on top
Turn off the warmer
Tell your manager, because it is in the danger zone
check.why: Hot food must stay at 135°F or above, so a reading of 120°F is in the danger zone.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Cooking, reheating and cooling temperatures
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Cook, reheat and cool food to the FDA Food Code's safe temperatures.
This lesson builds toward: When cooking, reheating or cooling food, you will choose the safe temperature and time for each food and plan fast cooling, matching the FDA Food Code numbers taught in the course.
Cooking to the right internal temperature kills germs. The FDA Food Code's main cooking temperatures for food service are: poultry (chicken, turkey) and stuffed foods: 165°F for less than 1 second (instant). Ground meat such as hamburger, and eggs that will be held for later: 155°F for 17 seconds. Whole cuts of beef and pork, fish, and eggs cooked for immediate service: 145°F for 15 seconds.
Reheating: cooked food that you cooled and will hot-hold must be reheated to 165°F for 15 seconds within 2 hours. Food cooked in a microwave should reach 165°F, be stirred and covered, and stand for 2 minutes.
Cooling: cooked food must cool from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours, and from 135°F to 41°F within 6 hours in total. Cool faster by dividing food into shallow pans, using an ice bath or ice wand, and stirring. Never leave a big stockpot to cool on the counter.
Your local health department may use a newer or older version of the Food Code, and home cooking advice differs (for example 160°F for ground beef at home). For an exam or a job, learn the numbers your course and your health department use.
Step by step:
- Check the thickest part with a thermometer.
- Poultry and stuffed foods: 165°F.
- Ground meat and eggs held for later: 155°F for 17 seconds.
- Whole cuts, fish, eggs for immediate service: 145°F for 15 seconds.
- Reheat for hot holding: 165°F for 15 seconds within 2 hours.
- Cool: 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, to 41°F within 6 hours total.
Words to know:
- Internal temperature: the temperature in the thickest part of the food, measured with a thermometer.
- Ice wand: a sealed plastic paddle filled with ice or water and frozen, used to stir and cool food fast.
- Two-stage cooling: cooling cooked food to 70°F within 2 hours, then to 41°F within 6 hours in total.
Official sources:
- FDA: Procedures for standardization of retail food safety inspection officers (Food Code cooking, reheating and cooling temperatures)
- FDA: Key temperatures for egg safety in food service
Try it now: Make a pocket card with the cooking, reheating, holding and cooling temperatures from this lesson. Then plan how you would cool a full pot of chili quickly, step by step.
You can now cook, reheat, hold and cool food to safe Food Code temperatures and check them with a thermometer.

check.q: What is the food service cooking temperature for a whole cut of beef or pork?
options: 145°F for 15 seconds
120°F for 1 minute
155°F for 17 seconds
165°F for 15 seconds
check.why: Whole cuts of beef and pork reach 145°F for 15 seconds under the FDA Food Code.

check.q: A full stockpot of rice must be cooled. What is the best first step?
options: Leave the pot on the counter overnight
Put the hot pot straight into the cooler with a lid
Divide the rice into shallow pans
Cover it with a towel
check.why: Shallow pans let food cool through the danger zone fast enough.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting your food handler card and passing the exam
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find your local food handler card rule and prepare for the exam.
This lesson builds toward: Before and during a job in food service, you will identify the illness symptoms you must report and find the food handler card rule where you work, naming the symptoms and the deadline, card length and accepted courses from your health department.
Food handler card rules differ by state and county. Some states require a card for most food workers; some leave it to counties or cities; some have no general rule. Your local health department or environmental health office will tell you what applies where you work.
Example: California. Under California Health and Safety Code section 113948, food handlers must get a California food handler card within 30 days after being hired by a food facility. The card is valid for three years, and the course must come from a training provider accredited by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). Some places are exempt, such as certain grocery stores and school cafeterias, so check with your county.
A food handler card is different from a food manager certification (such as the ServSafe Manager exam). Food handler courses are short and cover the basics in this course. Manager certification is longer, goes deeper, and is usually required for the person in charge.
To prepare: take an accredited course, go over each topic in this course, use the pocket card you made, and practice with questions you write yourself or that come with your course. Read every question carefully: words like "first", "best" and "never" matter.
Step by step:
- Search your state or county name plus "food handler card" and find the health department page (often ending in .gov).
- Write down the deadline after hire, how long the card lasts, and which courses are accepted.
- Choose an accredited course from the list your health department points to.
- Review handwashing, cross-contamination, temperatures, allergens and cleaning.
- Take the course and the test, and keep a copy of your card.
Words to know:
- Food handler card: proof that you finished a basic food safety course; required for food workers in some states and counties.
- ANSI: the American National Standards Institute, which accredits food safety training providers.
- Food manager certification: a more advanced food safety credential, usually for the person in charge of a kitchen.
Official sources:
- Sonoma County, California: Food handler card (30 days, three years, ANSI)
- California Department of Public Health: Retail food safety training (HSC 113948)
Try it now: Final task: write your Safe Shift Checklist (handwashing, storage, temperatures, cooling, allergy steps, clean and sanitize steps, illness symptoms to report). Then look up the food handler card rule for your state or county and write the deadline, how long the card lasts and which courses count at the top.
You can now find the food handler card rule where you work, choose an accepted course, and prepare for the exam.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Handwashing Handwashing steps or times are missing or wrong. Lists the full handwashing steps and at least six times to wash. Also says when to change gloves and how to handle ready-to-eat food. Storage and cross-contamination Raw food is stored above ready-to-eat food, or no separate tools. Shows the right shelf order and separate or sanitized boards and knives. Also covers labeling with name and date and storing chemicals below food. Allergy and sanitizing steps Allergy steps or the clean-and-sanitize order are missing. Lists the allergy steps and the order: scrape, wash, rinse, sanitize, air dry. Mentions test strips and the label's contact time for the sanitizer. Holding temperatures Holding temperatures are missing or wrong. Cold at 41°F or below and hot at 135°F or above, checked with a thermometer. Adds a check schedule and a log. Cooking and cooling Cooking or cooling numbers are missing or wrong. Gives the right cooking temperatures and both cooling time limits. Adds the reheating rule and how to cool food fast. Illness and local card rule No illness symptoms listed, or no card rule at the top. Lists the symptoms to report and the local card deadline, length and accepted courses. Names the health department page where the rule was found. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is the difference between a food handler card and a food manager certification?
options: They are the same thing
A handler card covers basics; manager certification goes deeper for the person in charge
A handler card is only for managers
Manager certification is shorter
check.why: Food handler courses cover the basics; manager certification is longer and usually needed for the person in charge.

check.q: You start a new kitchen job next week. How do you find your food handler card rule?
options: Ask a friend in another state
Assume there is no rule
Buy the first course you see online
Check your state or county health department's page
check.why: Rules differ by state and county, so the local health department is the source.
